title: First words
goal: Greet people, say yes and no, thank, apologise and choose the right 'you' for the person in front of you.
intro:
Malayalis are warm but not effusive with words: a smile, a nod and a sideways head tilt often do the work of 'hello' and 'thanks'. Still, a handful of words will carry you a long way.

Notice that Malayalam has **two different 'no's**: അല്ല *alla* ('it is not [that]') and ഇല്ല *illa* ('there isn't / didn't / doesn't'). We'll meet them properly in unit 2, but start noticing them now.

vocab.en: hello; greetings (formal, any time of day)
vocab.note: Said with palms together. Among friends, a simple ഹലോ or 'hi' is common.
Also spelled അതേ. Colloquially often just ആ (ā) or ഉം (um).
Negates 'X is Y': ഇത് ചായ അല്ല 'this is not tea'.
Negates existence and verbs: ചായ ഇല്ല 'there's no tea'.
Used less than English 'thanks' among family/friends; with service staff a smile is enough.
In speech, politeness is usually expressed with the verb ending (-ാമോ, -ൂ) or 'ഒന്ന്'.
Rarely said aloud; people say 'good morning' in English or just namaskāram.

vocab.en: never mind; it's nothing; no problem

vocab.note: To elders it can still sound blunt; people prefer titles like ചേട്ടൻ, ചേച്ചി, സാർ.
Used in formal speech, letters, TV interviews.

phrases.en: Hello, how are you? (lit. is it well?)
You're well, aren't you? (very common greeting)
Could you say it once more?

grammar.title: Word order: subject – object – verb
grammar.body:
Malayalam puts the **verb at the end** of the sentence. The usual order is Subject – (Time) – (Place) – Object – Verb: 'I tea drink', not 'I drink tea'. There are **no articles** (a/the); ഒരു *oru* 'one' can be used like 'a'.

Because nouns carry case endings, word order is fairly flexible for emphasis, but the verb almost always stays last. Questions keep the same order — you just add a question word or the question ending -ō.

examples.en: I drink / am drinking tea. (I tea drink)
I'll go to Kochi tomorrow. (I tomorrow Kochi-in go-will)

grammar.title: Which 'you'? നീ, നിങ്ങൾ, താങ്കൾ — and titles
grammar.body:
**നീ** *nī* is intimate: for close friends, younger siblings, children. Using it to a stranger or an older person is rude.

**നിങ്ങൾ** *niṅṅaḷ* is the plural 'you' and also a polite singular — safe with strangers of your own age or younger, shopkeepers, colleagues. Some elders still feel it is a bit direct.

**താങ്കൾ** *tāṅgaḷ* is formal and respectful (speeches, interviews, letters). In real life, Malayalis very often **avoid the pronoun altogether** and use a title instead: ചേട്ടൻ *chēṭṭan* ('elder brother', for an older man), ചേച്ചി *chēcchi* ('elder sister'), സാർ, മാഡം, or ടീച്ചർ.

The verb itself doesn't change for 'you' (see unit 2), but imperatives do: informal വാ *vā* 'come', polite വരൂ *varū* 'please come'.

examples.en: Where are you going? (to an older man, lit. 'where is brother going?')

dialogue.title: Meeting a neighbour
dialogue.setting: Anna, a visitor, meets Mr Thomas, an older neighbour, at his gate in Kottayam.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.native: ക്ഷമിക്കണം, എനിക്ക് കുറച്ച് മലയാളം മാത്രം അറിയാം.
lines.roman: kṣamikkaṇam, enikkŭ kuṟacchŭ malayāḷam mātram aṟiyām.
lines.en: Sorry, I only know a little Malayalam.

lines.speaker: Thomas
lines.en: No problem! Not bad — good Malayalam.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.en: Thank you very much. OK, bye for now.

culture: Malayalis rarely say 'thank you' to family or close friends — it can sound distant. 'Goodbye' is usually പോയിട്ട് വരാം *pōyiṭṭŭ varām* ('I'll go and come back') or simply ശരി *shari* ('OK then'), because saying just 'I'm going' (പോകുന്നു) sounds final and slightly inauspicious. The side-to-side head wobble means 'yes / OK / I'm listening'.
